papers.name: Paper 1: Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel
papers.covers: Section A is Macbeth: one question on a printed extract, then the play as a whole, 30 marks plus 4 for AO4 (spelling, punctuation, vocabulary and sentence structure). Section B is The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: one question on a printed extract, then the novel as a whole, 30 marks. No choice of question in either section, and no copy of the text: the papers are closed book, so every quotation beyond the extract comes from memory. 40% of the GCSE. In June 2024 the Macbeth extract was Act 1 Scene 7 and the question asked how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character; the Jekyll extract was from Chapter 2 and asked how Stevenson creates an atmosphere of fear and danger.

papers.name: Paper 2: Modern texts and poetry
papers.covers: Section A is An Inspector Calls: one essay from a choice of two, no extract, 30 marks plus 4 for AO4. Section B is the Power and Conflict cluster: one named poem printed on the paper, compared with one other poem from the cluster chosen by the student, 30 marks. Section C is unseen poetry: one poem printed, 24 marks for a question on it, then a second poem printed and 8 marks for comparing the methods of the two. Both questions in Section C are answered; 32 marks in all. 60% of the GCSE. Closed book, so the fourteen unprinted anthology poems are learned. In June 2024 the printed poem was Kamikaze and the question asked how poets present the ways people are affected by conflict.

commandWords.word: Starting with this extract / this conversation / this speech, explore how …
commandWords.meaning: The Paper 1 shape. Begin with the printed extract and work outwards to the whole text: the mark scheme's top level asks for a response to the task and the whole text, so an answer that never leaves the extract cannot reach it. Twenty-four of the thirty marks are AO1 and AO2 together, twelve each, so every point names a method as well as a moment.

Not what the character is like, but how the writer builds that impression: the words chosen, the stage directions, the structure, what other characters say. Present is the signal to write about methods and their effects.

commandWords.word: How does [the writer] use [a character] to …
commandWords.meaning: The character is a device. Ask what job Priestley gives the Inspector, or Shakespeare gives Banquo, in the play's argument, and answer with what that character says, does and provokes, and where in the play it happens.

An invitation to weigh it: a judgement is expected, with evidence on more than one side, and a conclusion that says how far. Agreeing completely, or listing points with no verdict, both stop short of the top levels.

The two bullets under every Paper 1 and Paper 2 Section A question are the shape of the answer: what the character says and does, and how the writer presents them, or the extract and then the whole text. Cover both, and let the bullets order the paragraphs.

Section B. One poem is named and printed; the other is your choice from the cluster. Compare means both poems in the same paragraph, on the same idea, method by method, not one poem then the other. The top level asks for a comparison that is critical and exploratory throughout.

commandWords.word: In [poem], how does the poet present …
commandWords.meaning: The 24-mark unseen question. The poem is printed and nothing is known about it, so read it twice, find its idea, then write about the choices that build that idea: word, image, sound, form, structure, the change across the poem. AO1 and AO2 only, twelve marks each: no context is wanted.

commandWords.word: What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use …
commandWords.meaning: The 8-mark unseen comparison, AO2 only. Methods, not ideas: the question already tells you both poems present the same idea. Two or three well-chosen comparisons of technique, each with a word or phrase from each poem, earn it in fifteen minutes.

Printed under the Macbeth and An Inspector Calls questions only. Four marks for spelling, punctuation and sentence control across the whole essay, awarded at the end. Consistent accuracy and a range of sentence structures reach the full four.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Read, understand and respond to texts: maintain a critical style, develop an informed personal response, and use textual references, including quotations, to support and illustrate interpretations. Twelve of the thirty marks on every extract, essay and comparison question, and twelve of the twenty-four on the first unseen question.

Analyse the language, form and structure used by a writer to create meanings and effects, using relevant subject terminology where appropriate. Twelve marks on every thirty-mark question, twelve on the first unseen question, and all eight on the second, so it is the largest objective in the qualification.

Show understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written. Six marks on each thirty-mark question, none on unseen poetry. Context earns when it explains something in the text, not as a paragraph of history on its own.

Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation. Four marks on the Macbeth question and four on the An Inspector Calls question, awarded on a three-band scale: threshold, intermediate and high performance.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Extract question on Macbeth or Jekyll and Hyde (30 marks, plus AO4 on Macbeth)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: A critical, exploratory argument that begins in the extract and ranges over the whole text by choice, not by accident: precise quotations from memory placed beside the printed ones, a fine-grained analysis of methods with terminology used because it helps, and context that explains a choice the writer made. The mark scheme calls this a conceptualised approach: the essay has an idea about the text, and every paragraph serves it.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Essay on An Inspector Calls (30 marks plus AO4)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: The character or theme is treated as Priestley's device, so every point says what the choice does for the play's argument, and a well-chosen quotation from the right act supports each one. Both bullets of the question are covered, the structure of the play (the arrival, the chain, the ending) is used as a method in its own right, and the context of 1912 seen from 1945 explains rather than decorates.

The second poem is chosen because it answers the question beside the named one, and the two are compared throughout: the same idea in both, then the methods that carry it, with judicious quotations from the unprinted poem recalled exactly. Form and structure are compared as well as language, and the poets' contexts appear where they explain a choice.

grade9ByQuestionType.questionType: Unseen poem (24 marks) and unseen comparison (8 marks)
grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: The poem's idea is stated in the first sentence, then the analysis moves through the choices that build it, including the shape of the poem and how it changes, with terminology used judiciously and effects explored rather than named. The 8-mark comparison stays on methods, sets a technique from each poem side by side, and stops when the marks are earned.
